newsitem.title: EAST TIMOR: E. Timor braces for controversial statue ceremony.
newsitem.headline: E. Timor braces for controversial statue ceremony.

text.p: Authorities in the capital of troubled East Timor on Saturday put finishing touches to preparations for a ceremony to bless a giant statue of Jesus Christ which has raised the ire of local residents.
The seaside city of 170,000 people was calm with little sign of Indonesia troops on the streets despite expectations of protests at Sunday's ceremony.

The towering statue of Christ, built for the mainly Roman Catholic territory by Indonesia, has aroused the anger of many East Timorese who see it as a symbol of their annexation by Indonesia 20 years ago.

Standing on a headland overlooking Dili Bay, the 27 metres (90 feet) high statue is a reminder that the former Portuguese colony is Indonesia's 27th province. It has been built with funds from Indonesia's state carrier Garuda.
A sharp thunderstorm on Saturday afternoon blew away banners and loudspeakers set up for the ceremony. Workers could be seen repairing the damage.
Residents said protests were likely at the ceremony on Sunday, though some thought they would be muted.

"There may be some (protest) banners," said one resident, who spoke on condition of anonymity. But he added that any demonstrations were likely to be in favour of Nobel laureate Bishop Carlos Belo rather than be political in nature.
Belo, who was awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize along with self-exiled East Timor resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta, is to celebrate Mass before leading priests in a blessing ceremony.
Indonesian security officials said they did not anticipate any problems. They said some 25,000 people were likely to attend the ceremony.
Sproadic protests against Jakarta's rule still erupt in East Timor, which was invaded by predominantly Moslem Indonesia in 1975 and annexed a year later.
The United Nations has not recognised Jakarta's rule over the territory and still sees Portugal as the administering power.
There are restrictions on foreign journalists visiting the territory. A group of 20 reporters from Jakarta have been given special permission to cover the statue ceremony.

Belo is also scheduled to address a news conference on Monday to explain his remarks to the German magazine Der Spiegel. Belo was quoted as saying that Indonesian soldiers treated East Timorese like "scabby dogs" and "slaves".
He has denied the remarks but the German magazine has stood by its story.
A storm of protest erupted in Indonesia over his remarks. Students in East Timor held five days of protests in support of Belo.
